source.title_on_document: AI as a cognitive collaborator: Assimilation and accommodation in human–machine teaming for innovation

supplement.where: Appendix A, p. 10 of this PDF (survey instruments). The text also mentions supplementary robustness analyses treating accommodation as a continuous variable (p. 5, Measures), which are not shown anywhere in the PDF.
supplement.holds: Appendix A lists survey items for cognitive strategy, emotional engagement, perceived performance, and technology acceptance. No extra outcome statistics. The robustness analyses with continuous accommodation are described but not reported.

paper_design_summary: 371 mid-career professionals in South Korea were assigned by stratified randomization to a 2 x 2 design: working alone or in dyads, with or without GPT-4 (AI arms first took a 45-minute prompt-engineering training module). All completed a 90-minute open-ended innovation challenge in a controlled virtual environment. Blind expert raters scored each solution for quality, novelty, and feasibility (10-point scale) and for cross-functional knowledge integration (1-7 balance index); emotions and cognitive strategy came from self-report surveys.

ai_tool.how_used: Participants in AI conditions completed a 45-minute module on prompt engineering and hands-on interaction with GPT-4, then used it freely during the 90-minute problem-solving phase; prompt histories were collected (p. 5, Procedures and Measures; p. 7 prompt examples).

task.description: Open-ended innovation challenge mirroring real organizational problems, e.g., developing a novel digital product, reimagining customer service processes, or integrating sustainability into an existing offering (p. 5).

eligibility.reason: People were assigned by stratified randomization to GenAI (GPT-4) or no GenAI, crossed with individual vs dyad work, on an open-ended innovation (idea generation) task (p. 5). Table 2 reports 371 people across four arms (p. 6). Blind expert raters scored each solution for quality, novelty, and feasibility (p. 5). Reporting is thin (no exclusions, no unit of analysis, Table 3 betas do not match Table 2 raw gaps), which matters for extraction but not for eligibility.

one_line_finding: In a randomized 2 x 2 experiment with 371 Korean professionals, GPT-4 access raised blind expert ratings of solution novelty (individuals 7.1 vs 5.8 on a 10-point scale; Table 3 GenAI beta = .44, SE .13, p < 0.01) and quality (7.3 vs 6.2; beta = .41, SE .12) (p. 6, Tables 2 and 3).
open_questions: Design class: the paper calls it a 'field experiment', but it ran 'in a controlled virtual environment' on an assigned 90-minute challenge rather than inside participants' ordinary work (p. 5); I coded lab_rct. A reviewer may prefer field_rct or online_rct.

Teams were dyads (p. 5), yet Team No AI has N = 95, an odd number (Table 2, p. 6). It is unclear whether team solutions were scored once per dyad or once per member, and so whether the unit of analysis is the person or the team. I coded unit = participant because Table 2 Ns count people.

Table 3 coefficients do not match the Table 2 raw gaps (e.g., quality: Table 2 individual gap 7.3 - 6.2 = 1.1 points vs Table 3 GenAI beta = .41). The paper does not say whether outcomes were standardized. Standardization basis must be resolved before computing effects.

The 'GenAI x Team' row in Table 3 is labeled as an interaction, but the text reads it as the Team-with-GenAI effect relative to all others ('teams using GenAI achieved the strongest results overall (beta = 0.58, p < .001)', p. 6). The reference group is unclear.
Table 6 (p. 8) reports 'Team effect: beta = 0.336, p < .001' for H1-2, which conflicts with Table 3's Collaboration (team) beta = .11, n.s. (p. 6).
ai_available_when_produced is 'mixed' at the outcome level because two of four arms had GPT-4; within each AI arm the output was produced with AI available, so the contrasts are with_ai.
No count at assignment and no exclusions are stated; 371 is recorded as analyzed (Table 2 Ns sum to 371).
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on the output: emotional change (pre-post self-reported positive and negative emotion on a 7-point scale; Table 2 deltas), cognitive strategy classification (assimilation vs accommodation, from self-report plus coded prompt histories), perceived performance and technology acceptance (Appendix A). Tables 4 and 5 (p. 7-8) report mediation by accommodation and moderated mediation by emotional engagement on quality, novelty, feasibility, and integration; these are mechanism analyses, not AI-vs-no-AI contrasts. Inter-rater reliability ICC2 = 0.51 (p. 5). No overall creativity rating and no diversity measure across people are reported. Primary outcome is not named; under codebook rule 2 for with_ai, novelty rated by experts (S1-O2) is the first available construct (no overall creativity), and the individual-arm contrast with its Table 3 SE is the most complete.
